paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: For most of human history, time was measured by the heavens. The day was defined by the rotation of the Earth, and the second, once it came to be needed, was simply a fraction of that day: one 86,400th part of the mean solar day. The definition seemed secure until the early twentieth century, when astronomers comparing records of ancient eclipses with modern observations concluded that the planet's spin is not uniform. Friction generated by the tides is gradually slowing it, while movements within the Earth's core and atmosphere add irregular fluctuations of a few thousandths of a second per day. A unit of measurement that depends on a wobbling planet, physicists came to recognise, is hardly a unit at all.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: A partial remedy arrived with the quartz clock, developed in the late 1920s. When an electric voltage is applied to a suitably cut quartz crystal, the crystal vibrates at a remarkably stable frequency, and counting those vibrations provides a far steadier beat than any pendulum. Quartz, however, has limitations of its own. No two crystals are exactly alike, so each clock must be calibrated individually, and the frequency drifts as the crystal ages and as the temperature around it changes. For a reference that would be identical everywhere, physicists turned instead to the atom.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The principle behind the atomic clock is that an atom of a given element can absorb or emit energy only in fixed amounts, each corresponding to radiation of one precise frequency. Every atom of caesium-133, wherever it is found, responds to the same frequency, and that frequency is not altered by age. The first practical caesium clock was built in 1955 by Louis Essen and Jack Parry at the National Physical Laboratory in Britain. Its accuracy so far exceeded that of astronomical methods that, in 1967, the second was formally redefined as exactly 9,192,631,770 cycles of the radiation associated with a particular transition in the caesium atom. Since 1972, occasional 'leap seconds' have been inserted into atomic time to keep it in step with the Earth's irregular rotation, although this practice is due to be abandoned by 2035.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The most accurate caesium clocks in service today are known as fountains. A cloud of caesium atoms is first slowed almost to a standstill by six intersecting laser beams, which chill it to within a few millionths of a degree of absolute zero. The lasers then toss the cloud gently upwards, so that it rises about a metre through a chamber filled with microwaves before falling back under gravity, passing through the microwaves a second time on its way down. A further laser then measures what proportion of the atoms have changed their energy state. If the microwave frequency is exactly right, that proportion reaches its maximum, and an electronic system continuously adjusts the frequency to keep it there. Because the cold atoms move so slowly, they can be observed for almost a second, and the resulting clocks would neither gain nor lose a second in roughly 300 million years.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Even this is no longer the limit. So-called optical clocks use atoms such as strontium or ytterbium, which respond to visible light rather than to microwaves. Since light oscillates tens of thousands of times faster than microwave radiation, each second can be divided far more finely, and the best optical clocks are thought to be stable enough that they would have drifted by less than a second had they been running since the origin of the universe. The international body responsible for units of measurement is widely expected to redefine the second on the basis of optical clocks in the early 2030s, although which element should be chosen remains a matter of debate.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Why should such precision matter outside the laboratory? The most familiar answer is satellite navigation. A receiver calculates its position by comparing the times at which signals left several satellites, each of which carries its own atomic clock. Since radio signals travel about 30 centimetres in a billionth of a second, a timing error of that size produces a positional error of the same order. The satellite clocks must also be corrected for effects predicted by Einstein's theories of relativity: because of the combined influence of weaker gravity and the satellites' speed, they gain around 38 millionths of a second each day relative to identical clocks on the ground, a discrepancy that, left uncorrected, would cause calculated positions to drift by roughly ten kilometres daily. Telecommunications networks, electricity grids and financial markets depend on the same signals.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: For physicists, however, the value of better clocks lies increasingly in what they might reveal. Relativity predicts that time passes more slowly where gravity is stronger, and the latest optical clocks are sensitive enough to register the difference when one of them is raised by just a few centimetres. Some researchers, among them the metrologist Anneke Voss of the Hallberg Institute, suggest that networks of such clocks could eventually be used to map variations in the Earth's gravitational field or to monitor the movement of molten rock beneath volcanoes. Whether these ambitions will be realised is uncertain: optical clocks remain delicate laboratory instruments, and moving them without degrading their accuracy is itself a formidable engineering problem. Yet the history of timekeeping suggests that each gain in precision has eventually found uses its inventors did not foresee.

questions.prompt: Historical records of eclipses helped to show that the Earth does not rotate at a constant rate.

explanation.correct: Astronomers 'comparing records of ancient eclipses with modern observations concluded that the planet's spin is not uniform'; 'not uniform' = not constant.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage states this directly in paragraph A.

evidence.quote: astronomers comparing records of ancient eclipses with modern observations concluded that the planet's spin is not uniform

questions.prompt: The frequency of a quartz crystal is unaffected by the conditions around it.

explanation.correct: The frequency 'drifts ... as the temperature around it changes', which contradicts 'unaffected by the conditions around it'.

distractors.why_wrong: The passage says the opposite: temperature changes make the frequency drift.
The effect of the surrounding temperature is stated explicitly.

evidence.quote: the frequency drifts as the crystal ages and as the temperature around it changes

questions.prompt: Essen and Parry originally designed their clock for use in navigation.

explanation.correct: The passage gives the date, place and builders of the first caesium clock and its accuracy, but says nothing about the purpose it was designed for.

distractors.why_wrong: Navigation is discussed only in paragraph F, about modern satellites, not as the purpose of the 1955 clock.
Nothing in the passage states a different purpose for the clock.

evidence.quote: The first practical caesium clock was built in 1955 by Louis Essen and Jack Parry at the National Physical Laboratory in Britain.

questions.prompt: Leap seconds are expected to remain part of atomic time for the foreseeable future.

explanation.correct: Leap seconds have been inserted since 1972, but 'this practice is due to be abandoned by 2035', which contradicts the statement.

distractors.why_wrong: The practice is due to end by 2035.
The planned end of leap seconds is stated directly.

evidence.quote: although this practice is due to be abandoned by 2035

questions.prompt: Ytterbium clocks have so far proved more stable than strontium clocks.

explanation.correct: Strontium and ytterbium are named only as examples of atoms used in optical clocks; the passage says which element to choose 'remains a matter of debate' but never compares their stability.

distractors.why_wrong: No comparison of the two elements' stability is made.
The passage does not say strontium is more stable either; it only says the choice is debated.

evidence.quote: although which element should be chosen remains a matter of debate
